statement: Cat has 4 marbles. Ben has 2 more marbles than Cat. Ann has 5 more marbles than Ben. How many marbles does Ann have?

choices.misconception: I found how many marbles Ben has and stopped there.
I added the 2 and the 5 and forgot to start from Cat's 4.
I added 5 to Cat's 4 and skipped the step through Ben.
I added up the marbles of all three children.

hints: Start with the child whose number you know.
Draw three bars. Cat's is known. Ben's bar is Cat's bar plus a piece, and Ann's bar is Ben's bar plus a bigger piece. Go one child at a time.
Ben has 4 + 2 = 6 marbles. Ann has 5 more than Ben, so add 5 to 6.

solutions.reliable: Cat has 4. Ben has 2 more than Cat, so 6. Ann has 5 more than Ben, so 6 + 5 = 11. The idea to keep: when each person is compared with the next, follow the chain one step at a time from the person you know.
solutions.elegant: Ann has 5 more than Ben, who has 2 more than Cat, so Ann has 2 + 5 = 7 more than Cat: 4 + 7 = 11. The idea to keep: differences along a chain add up.

whyOnTest: Comparison chains reward working one step at a time, and skipping the middle person is the trap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
